title: Hierarchical key provenance and emergency revocation protocol
creator: Aisha Kumar
description: Problem: Current token governance focuses on rotation and naming but lacks a provable, queryable provenance model that maps keys to organizational hierarchy (org -> team -> service -> environment). This makes scoped emergency revocations and forensics slow and error-prone. Proposal: Add a hierarchical provenance metadata layer to issued tokens plus an emergency revocation protocol (circuit-breaker) that supports revoking at any node in the hierarchy and automatically surfaces correlated audit logs for rapid incident response. Goals: (1) enable single-command revocation at org/team/service/environment scopes, (2) ensure tokens can be traced back to creator, policy, and rollout windows, (3) integrate revocation actions into audit logs and alerting to support forensics and compliance.
acceptance_criteria: Tokens issued via service/SDK include a provable provenance blob (signed metadata) containing org, team, service, environment, issuance_time, rotation_window, and creator_id.

Console and admin API support revocation at four hierarchy levels: org, team, service, environment. Revocations are propagated within 30s to runtime and SDKs observe a 1 minute maximum TTL for cached permissions.
An emergency_revocation API endpoint with RBAC guardrails is available and audited; invocation records actor, justification, scope, and pre/post counts.
Audit logs include correlation IDs linking issuance, usage spikes, and revocation actions; a prebuilt Kibana dashboard exists for incident response.
Unit and integration tests cover provenance parsing, revocation propagation, and rollback procedures; performance regression <5% on 95th percentile token issuance latency.
Security review completed and SME sign-off obtained before release.
Runbook and ops playbook for incident response published to Confluence and linked from the console.
design_decisions: Provenance stored as a compact signed JSON Web Token (provenance-jwt) attached to the token metadata to avoid large DB lookups for hot-path validation.
Revocation mirror: central revocation index plus per-region in-memory bloom filters for fast rejection without synchronous DB calls.
RBAC for emergency_revocation restricted to a new admin scope 'revoke:global' and audited separately from standard admin actions.
Retention: token issuance and revocation events retained in cold storage for 2 years to satisfy compliance requests.
Fallback: runtime will consult a 'soft-revoke' cache first; if uncertain it falls back to authoritative index to avoid false positives.
rollout_plan: Phase 1 (Canary - internal): Implement provenance-jwt and soft-revoke flow for internal services only. Duration: 2 weeks.
Phase 2 (Partner customers): Enable on select Dedicated customers with opt-in. Runbook validation and scaling tests. Duration: 3 weeks.
Phase 3 (GA): Roll out to hosted API with console controls and prebuilt audit dashboard. Enable RBAC guards and scheduled security review. Duration: 2 weeks.
Feature flag gating for provenance and emergency_revocation to allow fast rollback.
Post-GA: Collect metrics and iterate on propagation latency and false-positive rates for revocations.
monitoring_and_alerting: Alert: revocation-error-rate > 1% for 5m triggers SEV-2 and auto-rollbar link.
Metric: time-to-propagate (95th percentile) for revocation across regions; target < 60s.
Audit: dashboard showing issuance vs active tokens by scope with ability to pivot to user/credential and recent revocations.
Forensics view: prebuilt Kibana query that correlates provenance IDs, auth failures, and network metadata for last 48h.
Daily job that validates bloom filter drift vs authoritative index and alerts on divergence > 0.1%.
rollback_plan: Toggle feature flag to disable emergency_revocation and provenance-enforcement in runtime; this restores previous behavior immediately.
If revocation index becomes unavailable, runtimes fall back to authoritative check paths (slower) while an incident is declared and pager duty notified.
Post-rollback: run a reconciliation job to ensure no legitimate revocations were lost and notify affected teams.
Communications: status page update and customer notifications for any user-visible incidents.
Include automated run of unit tests and smoke tests before re-enabling feature flag.
open_questions: Should provenance-jwt include a hashed service config snapshot to aid debugging? Tradeoff: larger token size vs forensic richness.
What is the exact TTL for SDK cached decisions in offline clients? Proposal: 60s but need SDK team buy-in.
Do we expose bulk-revoke to partners or require manual support for cross-tenant revocation to avoid accidental mass deletion?
Legal/compliance requirements for long-term retention of provenance data in EU customers (GDPR records-of-processing)?
Operational load: how many revocation operations per second can the central index sustain before needing sharding?
